speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: asked the Minister for Manpower whether the Government will consider a temporary reduction of CPF contributions by both employee and employer till after the economy has recovered from the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) how common is the practice for employers and recruiters to ask job seekers to declare their last drawn salary or to share previous payslips; (b) whether any study has been made to ascertain how such practices affected employability and salary packages of job applicants; and (c) whether such a practice should be stopped so that applicants can move up the wage scale.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) arising from the COVID-19 situation, what is the employment status of Singaporeans who are currently based overseas; and (b) what are the assistance support available for them if they have lost their jobs and	would like to return to Singapore to seek employment

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: asked the Minister for Manpower (a) whether the introduction and implementation timeline of the new SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package will be impacted by the COVID-19 crisis and can be expedited; and (b) whether the at-risk mid-career workers can be given more transitional support during this steep economic slowdown.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked about our labour market situation in light of the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Total employment, excluding foreign domestic workers, registered its sharpest quarterly contraction since SARS, due primarily to a significant decline in foreign employment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Ang Hin Kee's question, there are about 200,000 Singaporeans living, working or studying abroad at any one time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our employment surveys do not generally cover these overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, given the global impact of the COVID-19 outbreak, we can imagine that some of them may face job losses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As our citizens, they will always be welcome home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will also do our best to help all Singaporeans, including those who return, and whether they are fresh graduates or mid-career individuals, all the support systems and services will be extended to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) and other schemes under the Unity, Resilience and Solidarity Budgets are helping to cushion the impact on the labour market.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Uncertainty about the future will also moderate hiring.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are therefore making a big push to open up pathways to jobs, including traineeships and skills upgrading programmes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will speak more on these measures during the debate on the Fortitude Budget.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given this backdrop, it is understandable that Mr Seah Kian Peng asks if the Government would consider a temporary reduction of CPF contributions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the objective is to reduce the cost burden to employers, JSS has done so with fewer drawbacks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, those who depend on CPF contributions to meet housing and healthcare needs can continue to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Singaporeans' ability to save for retirement is also not eroded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As an added advantage, JSS is able to target stronger support at sectors that are more affected by the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another avenue of support was offered by the National Wages Council (NWC).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Guidelines issued in March suggested that employers can consider reducing non-wage costs and making use of Government support measures such as the SkillsFuture Enterprise Credit to train and upskill workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The guidelines also advise employers to consider using the Monthly Variable Component (MVC) to adjust wages to save jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such a tripartite approach to managing cost pressures is not easily available in many countries.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nonetheless, we will continue to monitor and assess the situation, and consider whether other measures, including adjusting CPF contribution rates, may be necessary in future.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In these challenging times, there are also heightened sensitivities about fair treatment.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, when it comes to recruitment, Mr Saktiandi Supaat is concerned if job seekers have been forced to declare their last drawn salaries during job application.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, there is no rule that job seekers must comply, and employers cannot insist on it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We should, however, take a practical approach on whether employers are allowed to ask for such information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The last drawn salary is a relevant input to employers seeking to gauge a candidate's seniority or to make an appropriate job offer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, if employers use last drawn salary to screen applicants, they risk losing out on good candidates who are prepared to adjust their salary expectations, especially in today's context.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is similarly unwise for employers to overlook the longer track record of the applicant, and make an offer based solely on the last drawn salary especially if the last-held position was an interim one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If a job seeker chooses to provide salary information, employers should use it carefully.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Ms Joan Pereira asked about fair treatment of workers when they are retrenched, terminated, or have their wages reduced.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this challenging period, we recognise that both workers and employers have to make sacrifices to save jobs wherever possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides the NWC's guidelines on the fair approach to adjusting wages, the tripartite partners have issued advisories on managing excess manpower.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have been clear that retrenchment should be a last resort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the question of "disguised retrenchments", there are clear guidelines.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even during the COVID-19 period, whatever the termination of employment is called, an employee is presumed to have been retrenched if the employer cannot show a plan to fill the vacancy any time soon.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the retrenchment benefit is spelt out in the employment contract or collective agreement, the employer has a clear obligation to pay.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He cannot side-step it by calling the retrenchment something else.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, in today's context, the bigger challenge is not that the employer pretends it is not a retrenchment, but that he does not have the means to fulfil his obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The norms may have to be set aside in these abnormal times.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nevertheless, businesses should still give some support to retrenched employees, to the extent that they can afford.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through these notifications, MOM and TAFEP identify companies for further engagement, for example, if their planned wage cuts appear excessive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Following our intervention, many companies reviewed their cost-saving measures to give more wage support to employees.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our interventions also reveal that quite often, the worker suspects he has not been fairly treated because of poor communication with his employer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, an employee of a private pre-school operator was aggrieved to be asked to clear 13.5 days of her annual leave during the two-month long circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We found that she continued to get full pay even though her work hours were significantly reduced.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The employer had also seen a sharp drop in revenue due to school fee refunds and the JSS payout was insufficient to cover employees' full wages during the period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nevertheless, after MOM's engagement, the employer arranged for this employee to work more days and only clear six days of annual leave.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The company also took our advice to improve their communications by explaining their cost-saving measures clearly to all staff.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The cases we reviewed show that in the course of saving the business and preserving jobs, workers and employers need to build trust and maintain open communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The tripartite partners firmly believe in the principle of shared responsibility, and urge both employers and employees to work together during this difficult time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The general principles of fair treatment apply equally to all our workers, whether local or foreign.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Likewise, when companies have to reduce wages in order to save jobs, both local and foreign employees should be considered.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the unfortunate event of retrenchment, it would certainly not be right to expect employers to favour their foreign employees compared to local workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Government cannot also be expected to provide the same degree of fiscal support to employers to retain their foreign employees compared to their local employees, as Ms Anthea Ong seems to advocate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is not a question of fairness, but reasonableness.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With respect to disputes involving dismissals, salary payment or repatriation home, there are established processes for handling them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It should not matter whether the worker contracted COVID-19 or not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has also been a long-standing policy that employers have a duty to upkeep their workers until they have been repatriated home.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not new to employers and MOM has not seen an increase in the number of such disputes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In any case, migrant workers with issues can raise them to MOM and the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management through the Migrant Worker Ambassadors and the Forward Assurance and Support Team officers that are currently deployed at the dormitories.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We are very mindful that this period can be stressful to all workers and, of course, to our migrant workers as well, particularly those who are living in dormitories.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As detailed in my Ministerial Statement at the 4 May 2020 sitting of Parliament, we have made extensive efforts to disseminate information to them, in their native languages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many Non-Governmental Organisations (NGOs) have helped with volunteers manning hotlines and providing additional materials.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The National Jobs Council had our first meeting yesterday.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Chaired by Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam, the Council includes veteran business leaders from industries and union leaders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will focus on identifying and developing jobs, traineeships and skills training opportunities for Singaporeans amidst the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As pointed out by Senior Minister Tharman, the scale of our attempt goes beyond any past experience.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Complementing these efforts must be a renewed emphasis on fair opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is no less important, in my view.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The COVID-19 outbreak has only strengthened our resolve.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In these challenging times, it is all the more critical to give our people the assurance of fair recruitment.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think all businesses appreciate the Job Support Scheme and other reliefs that have been granted to them to help them reduce their cost and, to the extent possible, to save jobs.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the prospect of more job losses and, in fact, the prospect of wage cuts, is becoming more likely and prevalent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, that is the genesis behind the question which I asked, whether there could be a temporary reduction of employee's and employer's CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: While I appreciate and recognise that CPF indeed is a very important part of our overall financial planning, I would like to ask the Minister whether it is possible — I think on the employer side, fair enough, there is already enough support, but for most employees, the fact is that many of them are bringing back less.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Every little bit that we could put on the table for them is something which will certainly help them, particularly in the current climate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is an important part, I know the Minister had said that she will consider this, this is still on the table, but I think we need to do it a bit more proactively, given the looming and the likelihood of more wage cuts coming onstream.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I hope the Minister will put this as a high priority item, something to be activated earlier rather than later.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And, certainly, for the individual, there is very little likelihood that they can make up for what they were not able to grow in their CPF savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it is a decision that we have to take very carefully and certainly not lightly at all especially in consideration of the fact that our people will continue to live long lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If we continue to manage our healthcare well, that must still be the upside to having progress in our society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, we have to look at the longer term implications of any moves on the CPF front.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It may well come to a stage where we have to do something about it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I take Mr Seah's point very well that if we can be proactive than to be reactive to the situation, that is indeed what we are trying to do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If you think about not just the Unity, Resilient, Solidarity and Fortitude Budget provisions, which is to try and preserve jobs, we are at the same time not taking for granted that people who will become displaced will be able to move back into jobs easily, given the current situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why there is going to be a big push for many more pathways to jobs, which I will say more about later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Now that we are in an excess labour market situation, can I ask the Minister if we should now focus our skills upgrading, our traineeships in sectors and in companies that traditionally hire more EPs and S Passes?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In one particular aspect of the SGUnited Jobs and Skills package, we have identified Professional Conversion Programmes as an area of opportunity that could potentially benefit the employer as well as the job seeker.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Liang correctly points out, there have been areas where, for many years, companies have become quite used to filling actually quite good job positions with Employment Pass holders as well as S Pass holders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the built environment sector, for example, and I am looking at Minister Desmond Lee who is seated right in front of me, he and I have a joint interest, for example, in ensuring that good quality jobs that the built environment sector is creating, such as for building information modelling, these positions can actually be filled by Singaporeans – whether they are graduating from ITE, Polytechnics or even Universities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With appropriate training, they can actually take up these good jobs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What we need to do now is to work with the employers, work with the trade associations, to create the conversion programmes and then to reach out to suitable job applicants and put the match together.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think that is a very positive and the right way to go about trying to help job seekers and, at the same time, benefiting the employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: But I thought to further emphasise the point on contractual terminations, although the Employment Act does not prescribe the need for employers to give reasons for contractual terminations, whether with or without notice, whether MOM will want to push this agenda to advise and encourage employers to provide reasons for their termination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I think if the reasons are valid and if there is trust and proper communication with the employees, I am sure the employees themselves will understand the rationale and why they execute the contractual termination.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I understand where Mr Patrick Tay is coming from.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MOM is mindful that during these times, we have already been issuing many advisories to employers on a whole range of matters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would be quite careful and circumspect about issuing more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Frankly, employers themselves are under quite considerable pressure and we certainly do not want to enact more rules than is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The point really is this: between employers and employees, there should be good communication.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In certain instances where both sides are under pressure, this may break down.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our approach in handling these disputes is, firstly, to try and establish the facts and, secondly, to try and bring both parties to talk to each other.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Quite often, that gets the job done; and quite often, it is due to a misunderstanding of each other's intentions, even more so during such times.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But, I am quite mindful not to too easily jump to the conclusion that employers are trying to avoid their obligations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In normal times, perhaps there will be a number of such employers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But in these very, very abnormal times, I think the evidence suggests that it is more due to the fact that the employers are also trying but they themselves face a lot of difficulties.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad to hear her mention about the proactive measures that MOM has taken to address fair consideration given the current situation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What I am suggesting in my Parliamentary Question and also in this supplementary question, is about proactive measures beyond, for the post COVID environment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will give the example of the US congress.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It passed the Bill on Paycheck Fairness Act in 2019 to address the issue about indicating salary in job applications.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reason why I am raising this is because I am worried that, for example, fresh graduates in the post COVID environment are wary of taking up first jobs that pay below the median salary for fear that their salaries will always be pegged to it, particularly, those offered by SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is the post COVID environment that I am concerned about, whether we could be proactive in taking these steps ahead of this situation arising.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The fresh graduates would rather wait it out if they can rely on their parents, leading to months of post-graduation unemployment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My concern is whether some of the salary or payslip practices by employers will actually lead to further negative externalities in the future, thus exacerbating unemployment numbers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As it turned out, my previous job was as a HR director and in that role, I reviewed hundreds, perhaps thousands of job applications, which of course include information of all kinds: name, gender, last drawn pay, where you used to work, what you did in school, Co-curricular Activities (CCAs), what awards you had won, what membership you have.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think if I can share from a HR practitioner's perspective, the last drawn pay is really one of many things that is considered when we make a job offer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If a HR practitioner or a firm is so short-sighted as to look rigidly at the last drawn pay as an indication of the candidate's worth to the organisation, then my advice to the applicant is look for another employer, this is not a company that you should spend too much time on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: WSG, and actually our partners as well, will be more than happy to work with the job seeker to explore other options.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Do not spend too much time and waste your energy with these kinds of employers who cannot see beyond one number.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Before I ask the supplementary questions, can I put on record, given what the Minister had said, there was actually no intention and no implication on my part to say that employers treat local workers better than foreign workers.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Especially for myself, I am an employer of local employees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do not think it was fair to infer that was my implication from the question that I asked.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: And again, if this communication for the online process is also translated into their native languages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But as Ms Ong will also be aware, in the gazetted dormitories and subsequently in all the purpose-built dormitories, the Government put together staff teams to support the operations at the dormitories.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And that had included a provision of food as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, that part of it I think, has been clear.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Ong mentioned miscellaneous expenses, I am not entirely sure what other miscellaneous expenses they include, but if it has to do with the upkeep of the workers, then the answer is yes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It depends on what those cost items are.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Back to her first question, on whether the online processes are available in native languages, the online application itself may not be, but then it is also not available in Chinese, in Malay or in Tamil.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But what is important is that access to those channels is not impeded by language barriers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For that, we work together with our partners – the Migrant Workers' Centre, for example, has got not just staff but also a very large pool of volunteers and these volunteers can include the migrant workers themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, most often, they are the migrant workers themselves.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When a worker comes to work in Singapore for the first time, they go through a settling-in programme and the migrant workers' ambassadors are also familiar, or at least we continuously reach out through them, to remind workers of which are the avenues that they have to raise their concerns.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many Non-governmental Organisations (NGOs) also establish links with these workers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad, engages these NGOs on a very regular basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have worked out a system where regardless of where these workers are housed, they are able to provide feedback and raise their concerns with us so that we can address them properly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If language turns out to be a barrier, we have no shortage of people who are able to come in to intermediate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The process may take a little bit longer, but it can be done.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And finally, I appreciate Ms Ong's clarification on her intent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have a question for with regard to the declaration of last drawn salary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that California has banned this, I think in January 2018.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Although, I think there are many other contributing factors that are more prominent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have a lot of things on our plate.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Useful studies, we will take a look at them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it will not be realistic to chase down every study.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have to just be circumspect about which are the avenues that are worth pursuing.
